cloud-operating-model.outcome: Take one deployable service you run (or the seed search-index service) and produce deployment_incident_repair_packet.md: the operating model for shipping it safely — rollout, rollback trigger, health check, telemetry signal, and the runbook step that turns a bad deploy into a fast recovery instead of a 2 a.m. guessing game.
cloud-operating-model.proof: deployment_incident_repair_packet.md attached to the evidence ledger, containing: context, assumptions, selected approach, rejected approach, expected failure, verification method (a kubectl rollout transcript + a metric snapshot), a reviewer objection, repair notes, and the capstone connection. A reviewer can trace one deploy from push → health-gate → live, and one rollback, without you narrating.
cloud-operating-model.unlock: Your packet names the rollout strategy, the exact rollback trigger (an SLO breach, not a hunch), the health check that gates traffic, and the telemetry you would read first during an incident.
cloud-operating-model.doNotClaim: Do not claim a 'cloud operating model' if your packet only describes the happy-path deploy. An operating model that has no named rollback trigger and no telemetry signal is a deploy script wearing a suit. The model is defined by how it FAILS safely, not how it ships on a good day.

cloud-operating-model.text: A deploy goes out at 16:50 on a Friday. Error rate climbs from 0.2% to 6%, the SLO burns, and three engineers start arguing about whether to roll back while customers see stale search results — because nobody agreed in advance what a bad deploy even looks like, or who pulls the cord.

The cloud operating model is the foundation lesson of Course 05: it is the contract that ties together containers, Kubernetes rollout, health checks, observability, and incident response into one repeatable loop. Everything downstream — canary, SLOs, runbooks — is an instance of this loop, so we build the loop first as a reviewable packet.

cloud-operating-model.prompt: Your deployment.yaml has readinessProbe and livenessProbe both pointing at GET /health, which returns 200 as soon as the process boots. The deploy goes 'green' in kubectl, but users get errors. What did the operating model get wrong? Answer before reading on.
cloud-operating-model.reveal: The health check lied. /health returned 200 before the service could actually serve traffic — DB pool not warm, index client not connected — so Kubernetes marked pods Ready and shifted live traffic onto them. 'Ready' must mean 'can serve a real request', not 'process is alive'. A liveness probe answers 'should I restart this?'; a readiness probe answers 'should I send traffic?' — conflating them turns your rollout gate into a rubber stamp, and a green kubectl rollout into a silent outage.

cloud-operating-model.title: An operating model is a closed deploy loop: gate, observe, reverse
cloud-operating-model.text: Define how a change reaches production (rollout strategy + readiness gate), how you SEE it behaving (telemetry tied to an SLO), and how you UNDO it (a named rollback trigger and command). The invariant: every deploy has a reversal path proven before you need it.

cloud-operating-model.title: The deploy loop — and its two paths through an incident
cloud-operating-model.subtitle: Push → CI → rolling deploy gated by the readiness probe → live traffic, watched by telemetry. The SLO breach is the decision: healthy continues; breach forces the rollback path. Payments and auth are out of scope.

legend.label: telemetry + the SLO that triggers rollback

cloud-operating-model.title: The operating model as config + the rollback transcript
cloud-operating-model.subtitle: deployment_incident_repair_packet.md embeds the real artifact: a Deployment with an honest readiness gate, plus the kubectl proof of a safe reverse.
cloud-operating-model.code:
# Rollout strategy: never replace all pods at once.
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 }

# Readiness gate: 'Ready' must mean 'can serve a real request'.
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10 }

# Rollback trigger (the cord): error-rate SLO burns > 2% for 2 min.
# Proof of a safe reverse — captured live, pasted into the packet:
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/search-index
Waiting for rollout: 2 of 4 updated replicas available...
error: deployment exceeded progress deadline   # bad image never went 100%
$ kubectl rollout undo deploy/search-index
deployment.apps/search-index rolled back
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/search-index
deployment "search-index" successfully rolled out   # last-good restored

steps.label: Rolling, never big-bang
steps.note: maxUnavailable: 0 means old pods keep serving until new ones pass the gate. A bad image degrades a slice, not the whole service.

steps.label: Readiness = serve, not boot
steps.note: /readyz checks the DB pool and index client are actually connected. This is the gate the pretest's /health failed to be.

steps.label: Liveness = restart, not traffic
steps.note: /livez answers a different question: is the process wedged and worth killing? Conflating the two turns the rollout green while users get 500s.

steps.label: The named trigger
steps.note: The rollback cord is an SLO breach with a threshold and a window — not 'it feels bad'. This is the line that makes it an operating model.

steps.label: The gate caught it
steps.note: Because maxUnavailable was 0 and the gate was honest, the bad image hit the progress deadline instead of 100% of traffic.

steps.label: The proven reverse
steps.note: kubectl rollout undo restores the last-good ReplicaSet. This transcript IS the verification evidence the packet requires.

cloud-operating-model.caption: A reviewer should read this and trace both paths: a deploy that gates safely, and a breach that reverses in one command.

cloud-operating-model.text: Standards grounding (DORA 2024): the four keys — deploy frequency, lead time, change-fail rate, and failed-deployment recovery time — are all properties of THIS loop. Elite teams are not the ones who never break prod; they are the ones whose operating model makes recovery boring. A named rollback trigger plus a proven undo is what moves your change-fail recovery from hours to minutes.

cloud-operating-model.question: A reviewer asks: 'Show me the exact evidence this operating model survives a bad deploy, not just a good one.' Which artifact answers the challenge?
options: A clean kubectl rollout status showing a successful green deploy.
A kubectl rollout undo transcript triggered by a named SLO breach, plus the metric snapshot that fired it and the readiness gate that contained the blast radius.
A README paragraph explaining that the team 'follows DevOps best practices'.
A screenshot of the CI pipeline passing all unit tests.
cloud-operating-model.explanation: The reviewer asked for failure-path evidence. Only option 2 proves the loop reverses under a real breach: the metric that tripped the trigger, the gate that limited damage, and the undo that restored last-good. A green deploy (1), a prose claim (3), and passing tests (4) are all happy-path — none show the model recovering, which is the property the whole lesson exists to prove.

cloud-operating-model.title: Two deploy practices, same Kubernetes
cloud-operating-model.subtitle: Both 'use CI/CD and Kubernetes'. Only one is an operating model.

left.label: Deploy-and-pray
lines: kubectl apply, watch for the word 'green'
Rollback = 're-deploy the old branch' (minutes of guessing)
Telemetry = tail the logs after a customer complains
No threshold for 'bad' — it is an argument each time
left.verdict: Recovery time = however long the debate lasts

right.label: Operating model
lines: RollingUpdate, maxUnavailable 0 — old pods serve until gate passes
Rollback = kubectl rollout undo to last-good ReplicaSet (one command)
SLO + burn-rate alert fires before customers do
Trigger is written down: error-rate > 2% for 2 min → undo
right.verdict: Recovery is boring, fast, and rehearsed

cloud-operating-model.caption: Stale search results that recover in 90 seconds are an incident note; the same failure debated for 40 minutes is a postmortem. The difference is entirely in the operating model, not the cluster.

cloud-operating-model.intro: Prove your packet is an operating model, not a deploy script:
items: Your readiness probe checks something that can FAIL when the service cannot serve real traffic (DB pool, downstream client) — not just that the process booted. If /readyz can only return 200, it is not a gate.
Liveness and readiness answer different questions: name what /livez restarts and what /readyz gates. If they hit the same endpoint, fix it.
The rollback trigger is a written threshold + window tied to an SLO (e.g. error-rate > 2% for 2 min), not 'when it looks bad'.
You captured a real kubectl rollout undo transcript that restored the last-good ReplicaSet — paste it; do not describe it.
The packet names the blast radius (stale search ≠ data loss) and one out-of-scope boundary (e.g. payments path), so urgency is calibrated.

prompts: Explain, using your own packet, why a liveness probe and a readiness probe must answer different questions — and what breaks when they are the same endpoint.
Walk a junior through your rollback trigger: what number fires it, over what window, and what command they run at 2 a.m. without thinking.
Connect your loop to one DORA key: which of deploy frequency, lead time, change-fail rate, or recovery time does your rollback evidence most directly improve, and why?

cloud-operating-model.text: The loop is invariant across runtimes and risk profiles — only the dials change. On a low-traffic internal tool the rollback trigger can be loose and manual; on a regulated payments path the same model demands a canary, automated burn-rate alerts, and a tighter SLO, because the feared failure shifts from 'stale results' to 'lost money'. Serverless or VM, the three parts hold: gate the rollout, observe against an SLO, prove the reverse. The capstone reuses this exact deployment_incident_repair_packet.md — you will replay the search-index incident, trip the trigger, roll back, and attach the kubectl transcript and metric snapshot as your portfolio claim: not 'I understand cloud ops', but 'here is a deploy I shipped, broke, and recovered in one command — read the evidence.'
